scope: Rice editorial revision; existing measurements and baseline calculations reused
direction: Toward clearer source-supported interpretation; no certification thresholds changed

before.text: Rice can contain [[metals/arsenic-inorganic|inorganic arsenic]] and cadmium, with concentrations that vary by growing conditions, grain form and preparation. This review also covers lead, nickel, chromium and mercury where rice-specific evidence is available. Historical surveys describe the rice sampled at that time, so they cannot provide a universal rice concentration or rank current suppliers.

after.text: Use this review to compare a rice result with the available occurrence evidence, investigate sourcing differences and select controls to verify. The profile covers inorganic and total arsenic, cadmium, lead, nickel, chromium and mercury where measurements are available. Grain, cooked rice and derived foods retain their own measurement bases.

before.text: Choosing a control means looking at arsenic and cadmium together. Water management can lower arsenic while increasing cadmium in some soils, though this does not happen everywhere. Both need to be monitored under the relevant growing conditions. Milling and cooking can also change contaminants and nutrients in different ways. Buyers can use the [supplier brief](#from-historical-surveys-to-current-lots) and [dated requirement comparisons](#rice-requirements) to identify what to check for the delivered material and its intended use. Household guidance addresses suitable preparation and dietary variety, with separate precautions for infant feeding.

after.text: The most consequential control decision is often the joint response of arsenic and cadmium: a water regime that lowers one can raise the other, while some field settings show lower arsenic without a statistically detected cadmium increase. The evidence below identifies where that distinction changes a sourcing or processing decision.

before.text: This is still a partial assessment. Some comparisons remain uncertain because source details are unresolved, studies share samples, or measurements of what remains after treatment are incomplete. Historical surveys and experiments cannot establish current lot performance. Food concentrations and exposure biomarkers alone also cannot establish an individual health effect.

before.text: This page covers edible rice grain, including brown, white and cooked rice. Brown rice retains the bran and germ; polishing removes outer tissues to produce white rice. Grain fractions, prepared foods and rice-derived ingredients need separate interpretation because processing can change both composition and measurement basis.

after.text: This page covers edible brown, white and cooked rice. Brown rice retains the bran and germ; polishing removes outer tissues. Flour, bran, syrup, protein ingredients and drinks have separate processing and composition evidence. Uncooked grain describes a food form; dry weight describes an analytical moisture basis.

before.text: Flour, bran, syrup, protein powder and beverages are distinct materials. Their results can inform a grain assessment, but they cannot be assigned to untested rice products using a common conversion factor.

after.text: Flour, bran, syrup, protein powder and beverages are distinct materials. Their results can inform a grain assessment, but they cannot be assigned to untested rice products using a common conversion factor.

before.text: Use the material, chemical species and preparation reported in each study. The table below defines the main boundaries; the later sections explain occurrence, processing and controls in detail. Uncooked rice is a food form; a moisture-free dry-weight result is an analytical basis. The two descriptions are not interchangeable.

cells: Brown and white grain
Keep grain fraction and cultivar explicit. Matched brown/white measurements show that metals do not all respond alike to polishing.
Cooked rice
Prepared-food composites describe the sampled food after preparation. Compare concentrations only on a compatible moisture and preparation basis.
Derived ingredients and foods
Syrup, protein, flour, drinks and specialized formulas require their own composition and preparation evidence. Grain results do not establish the final product concentration.

passages.text: For this parent page, derivative studies explain where grain evidence stops transferring. A drink, specialized formula or protein powder must retain its own formulation, processing and preparation instructions. Rice drinks and medically formulated infant feeds are distinct products; their measurements should not be substituted for one another.

before.text: Origin can inform investigation, but its meaning depends on the survey. Carey’s and Shi’s international studies target market rice with unequal geographic coverage, whereas the FDA regions are collection markets. A US collection-region label does not identify growing origin. Country and region differences can also reflect cultivar, milling, water management, harvest period and detection-limit treatment, so they cannot be read as fixed properties of all future shipments.
before.heading: Geography and sampling frame

after.text: Origin helps identify sourcing options to investigate. International rice surveys show variation between and within sampled countries, but cultivar, milling, water management and harvest conditions also contribute. Confirm whether a location means growing origin or collection market: FDA collection regions describe where foods were purchased, not where the rice was grown.
after.heading: Origin and sourcing

before.text: Cultivar studies demonstrate that genetics matters within a defined environment. Liu’s ionomic association study examines rice accessions under contrasting growing conditions, and Tran’s Vietnamese landrace study measures both brown and white grain. Genetic associations identify candidate loci and breeding hypotheses; stable low accumulation requires confirmation across soils, water regimes and seasons while retaining acceptable yield and essential-element uptake. The number of accessions is not a number of independent studies.
before.heading: Cultivar, environment and changing conditions

passages.text: Muehe’s greenhouse experiment examines climate and soil arsenic together and finds that their combined effects can alter rice yield and grain arsenic. It is a treatment-specific experiment, not a prediction that every future crop will show the same percentage change. It strengthens the case for testing cultivar performance under the growing conditions in which it will actually be used.
passages.question: What does the climate experiment tell us about future crops?

after.text: Select a cultivar for the conditions in which it will be grown. Liu’s contrasting-environment study and Tran’s paired brown/white grain study show that genetic and grain-fraction differences matter, but a low result in one setting does not establish stable performance across soils, irrigation regimes and seasons. A useful supplier comparison retains these conditions alongside grain measurements.
after.heading: Cultivar and growing conditions

before.text: The FDA comparison calculates a matched historical change rather than a national trend. Across five shared winter-region groups, cooked white-rice cadmium medians change from 4.3 to 5.0 µg/kg and brown-rice medians from 5.5 to 9.8 µg/kg between FY2018 and FY2020. The matching uses six earlier and five later composites. The drawer retains the unmatched source summaries, so readers can distinguish the comparison subset from the full dataset.

passages.text: Within-lot and between-lot variability remain separate purchasing questions. Composite surveys smooth some individual-item variability, and repeated analytical runs improve measurement precision without creating new independent lots. A supplier claim needs current, identifiable lots and a sampling design suited to the shipment or process decision; a historical country median cannot replace that evidence.

after.text: Collection year can matter when growing conditions, sourcing or processing change. Compare periods with a compatible sampling design. In five shared winter-region groups, FDA cooked white-rice cadmium medians changed from 4.3 to 5.0 µg/kg and brown-rice medians from 5.5 to 9.8 µg/kg between FY2018 and FY2020. The comparison uses six earlier and five later composites; it describes these matched samples, not a national trend.

passages.text: Use the year and region controls to inspect the available matched comparisons. For a purchasing decision, request the supplier’s own harvest and lot history as well: a change in historical survey samples does not identify a change at that supplier.

after.heading: Collection year

before.text: Brown and white rice do not have one universal contaminant ranking. Polishing redistributes material between edible white grain and removed fractions. Tran’s matched brown/white analysis shows that many elements decline with polishing, while cadmium does not follow the same pattern. This prevents a blanket “polishing removes heavy metals” conclusion. Bran and other by-products also need characterization if they enter human food, supplements or feed; the metal removed from one fraction has not necessarily left the wider food chain.
before.heading: How do brown and white rice compare?

passages.text: The Vietnamese landrace experiment measured brown and white grain from the same plants. Most measured elements were higher in brown grain, but cadmium and molybdenum were exceptions. This is stronger evidence about the effect of grain fraction than a retail comparison of unrelated brown and white products. It also shows why an arsenic benefit from polishing cannot automatically be assigned to cadmium.
passages.question: What does the matched brown-versus-white comparison add?

after.text: Polishing can lower arsenic and many other elements, but it is not a reliable universal cadmium control. Tran’s study measured brown and white grain from the same plants: most measured elements were higher in brown grain, while cadmium and molybdenum were exceptions. That paired design is more informative about milling than comparing unrelated retail products. Test the retained grain and the removed bran if both enter the food or feed chain.
after.heading: How do brown and white rice compare?

before.text: The table below groups rice controls by where they can be applied: agronomic measures during cultivation, manufacturing controls during sourcing and processing, and consumer choices during preparation and consumption. It brings together measured interventions, market comparisons and agency guidance, with their different scopes and limitations.

after.text: Choose the stage where the control can act: before harvest, during manufacture or during food preparation. The table distinguishes measured interventions, sourcing comparisons and agency guidance.

before.text: The best contaminant result depends on what else is measured. Drier irrigation can lower arsenic and mercury species and methane while increasing cadmium; the same management change may also affect yield and micronutrients. A cadmium increase is conditional: the Arkansas production-field comparison found no significant water-management effect on grain cadmium. Paired grain monitoring is therefore more informative than assuming that every drying regime shifts contamination toward cadmium. These linked outcomes explain why optimizing only arsenic can give a misleading assessment of the crop. A treatment with a large percentage reduction can still leave an important residual concentration.
before.heading: Contaminants, nutrients and yield

passages.text: A yield benefit is not evidence of a contaminant benefit. Gupta’s ash trials are a useful counterexample: increased yield accompanied no statistically detected change in the measured grain arsenic species or cadmium. Conversely, a contaminant reduction with a yield penalty may be difficult to sustain. Both findings belong in the assessment rather than selecting only favorable endpoints.

after.text: The useful conclusion is conditional: a control should improve the measured food under its intended operating conditions. These findings change what needs to be checked before adopting it.
after.heading: Where findings agree, and where they differ

table.title: Findings that change a rice control decision

cells: Water management: arsenic and cadmium can move in opposite directions

Limmer and Seyfferth report lower arsenic with higher cadmium under drier management. The Arkansas production-field comparison found lower inorganic arsenic without a statistically significant cadmium response. Measure both in harvested grain under the proposed regime; a cadmium increase is possible, not inevitable.
Polishing: the response differs by element

Tran’s paired brown/white samples show that many elements decline with polishing, while cadmium is an exception. Verify the target analyte in the retained grain and characterize bran if it enters another food or feed stream.
Yield: more grain does not demonstrate less contamination
Gupta’s ash trials increased yield without a statistically detected change in measured grain arsenic species or cadmium. Keep yield and contaminant outcomes separate in a supplier’s efficacy claim.
Cooking: lower arsenic can accompany nutrient losses

Excess-water cooking can reduce inorganic arsenic; FDA guidance also identifies losses of nutrients from enriched rice. Check the tested preparation and what remains in the food rather than transferring the largest reported reduction to every process.

before.text: Polishing and water-intensive cooking can change both contaminants and nutrient composition. The brown/white comparison cannot determine an overall nutritional preference from one arsenic value, and cooking that leaches arsenic can also leach minerals or added nutrients. Net benefit requires the actual diet, food substitution and retained nutrient composition, not an unweighted sum of metal concentrations.

passages.text: Selenium applications illustrate another distinction: an agronomic Cd response, grain selenium enrichment and a clinical benefit are separate outcomes. The field experiment supports investigation of the tested control, while its transfer to commercial enriched rice needs direct grain measurements and nutritional assessment. More of an essential element does not establish less of another contaminant.

after.text: Selenium application, grain selenium enrichment and reduced grain cadmium are separate outcomes. Jiang’s field experiment supports investigation under its tested conditions; transferring the treatment to commercial enriched rice requires direct grain measurements and nutritional assessment.

before.text: Water demand, energy, sensory quality, amendment quality and waste handling can determine whether a laboratory process is usable. Chemical soaking creates different operating and disposal requirements from household cooking. Microbial or sorbent removal must also show that food quality and safety remain acceptable. Comparative commercial cost-effectiveness and complete mass balances are not established across the selected controls, so a universal preferred process cannot be assigned.

after.text: For manufacturing controls, compare the residual concentration with water and energy use, food quality and waste handling. Chemical soaking has different operating and disposal requirements from ordinary cooking. Complete mass balances and comparative commercial costs remain unavailable across the selected controls; those omissions prevent a universal cost-effectiveness ranking.

before.text: Sampling should match the decision. An increment, a composite, an analytical replicate and an independent lot are different units. The FDA composites describe prepared-food sampling; Shi’s compilation describes market grain; field treatment plots address agronomic response. None directly supplies a validated acceptance plan for a current shipment. The relevant unresolved quantities include within-lot heterogeneity, between-lot variation and uncertainty around the decision boundary.
before.heading: Representative material before analytical precision

after.text: A useful laboratory report connects the measured sample to the lot being purchased. Check how increments were taken and combined, which rice form was tested, and whether the sampling covers the shipment. Repeated analyses of one composite assess analytical precision; they do not measure variation between untested bags or lots.
after.heading: Representative material before analytical precision

before.text: Speciation needs demonstrated recovery and stability in the actual matrix. Navaretnam’s white/brown-rice method and Tian’s inorganic-arsenic assay show distinct analytical approaches. A sensitive instrument or a high calibration correlation does not alone establish extraction completeness, species preservation or agreement at the concentration where a purchasing decision will be made. Matrix validation, blanks, reference materials, recovery and reporting limits remain essential. The [[testing/icp-ms|ICP-MS methods overview]] explains the distinction between elemental measurement and chromatographic speciation.
before.heading: Species preservation and screening fitness

passages.text: Song’s Cr(VI) method found no detectable Cr(VI) in the small set of tested foods, including rice flour, and showed that recovery depended on whether the spike was introduced before or after extraction and on holding time. This illustrates a species-stability problem: nondetection must be bounded by the tested matrix, method and handling. It cannot prove that all rice is free of Cr(VI).

EFSA similarly notes that acidic extraction can convert thiolated arsenic species into DMA. A chromatographic result may therefore depend on sample handling as well as the original food composition. For transformation studies, recovering total arsenic does not by itself establish that each original species was preserved.
passages.question: Can sample preparation change the reported arsenic species?

after.text: Request the species needed for the decision, with matrix validation, recovery, reporting limits and uncertainty. A total-arsenic result does not supply measured inorganic arsenic. The [[testing/icp-ms|ICP-MS methods overview]] explains how elemental measurement differs from chromatographic speciation.
after.heading: Species preservation and screening fitness

passages.text: Song’s Cr(VI) method found no detectable Cr(VI) in its small food sample, including rice flour, but recovery depended on extraction and holding time. EFSA also describes conversion of thiolated arsenic species to DMA during acidic extraction. Ask whether the method preserves the species being reported and whether the reporting limit answers the purchasing question.
passages.question: Can sample preparation change the reported species?

before.text: Portable screening can help target confirmatory analysis, but its decision errors matter. Tian’s magnetic-purification electrochemical grain assay addresses matrix interference before measuring Cd and Pb; the purification occurs in the analytical workflow. Rice-specific bias, uncertainty, false acceptance and false rejection near the relevant boundary are needed before a screening result can substitute for a reference method in a lot decision.

passages.text: A non-detect means the result is below a stated analytical limit under that method. It is not a measured zero, and an unspecified limit cannot establish a useful upper bound. A nonsignificant treatment comparison answers a different question again: it may reflect little effect or imprecision. Neither statement means that a literature search found no relevant evidence.
passages.question: How should a non-detect differ from “no effect” in a report?

table.title: Checks for an interpretable rice test report
headers: What the report needs to establish

cells: Material and sampling
Identify the lot or survey, grain form and preparation. Describe increments, compositing, sample reduction and retained samples; analytical repeats do not measure unobserved lot variability.
Analyte and basis
Name the measured chemical species, units and moisture or preparation basis. Total-element results cannot silently replace a species-specific result.
Method performance
Document matrix validation, extraction recovery, species stability, blanks, reference materials and reporting limits. Calibration correlation alone is insufficient.
Decision uncertainty
Distinguish sampling from analytical uncertainty. A screening method needs evidence about bias and false acceptance or rejection near the intended decision boundary.

after.text: Portable screening can help select samples for confirmatory testing when its performance in rice is established. Tian’s magnetic-purification assay removes analytical interference before measuring cadmium and lead; it does not decontaminate the food. Check bias and false acceptance or rejection near the intended decision boundary before using screening for lot release.

passages.text: A non-detect means the result is below a stated analytical limit under that method. It is not a measured zero, and an unspecified limit cannot establish a useful upper bound. A nonsignificant treatment comparison answers a different question again: it may reflect little effect or imprecision. Neither statement means that a literature search found no relevant evidence.
passages.question: How should a non-detect differ from “no effect” in a report?

before.text: Use historical origin evidence to decide where to investigate, then qualify the actual material. The arsenic and cadmium surveys show variation within and between growing regions, with sampling limitations and reused observations. A current supplier dossier should identify cultivar, growing origin, harvest, grain form, milling, water management where known and delivered-lot identity. A country label alone cannot demonstrate the joint iAs/Cd/Hg composition of a shipment.
before.heading: What should a buyer request from a supplier?

after.text: Request evidence for the rice being delivered: lot identity, growing origin, harvest, cultivar, grain form, milling and water management where known. Use historical country evidence to investigate alternatives, then compare actual supplier lots on a compatible basis. A country label alone does not establish their arsenic, cadmium or mercury composition.
after.heading: What should a buyer request from a supplier?

before.text: Commercial evidence should be assessed rather than assumed absent. Li’s regional programme demonstrates a longer implementation horizon, while Sun and Jiang provide multiyear field observations. The remaining purchasing questions are narrower: which farms and lots were actually sampled, what residual concentrations and uncertainty were observed, how the practices persisted, and what they cost under the buyer’s conditions. Programme reach is not the same as the number of independent sampled farms.

after.text: For a claimed control, request its starting and residual grain measurements, sampled farms and lots, duration, yield and operating cost. Li’s regional programme and Sun’s and Jiang’s multiyear field observations provide implementation context, but programme reach is not the number of independently sampled farms. Use these details to judge whether the reported benefit transfers to the purchase.

before.text: Bioaccessibility, absorption and chemical extraction are different endpoints. An in-vitro digestion experiment measures what becomes soluble under its specified gastrointestinal model; human absorption requires biological evidence. Cardini’s methods study identifies cadmium-binding compounds using chemical extraction and chromatographic techniques. A low extraction yield in that workflow cannot be used as a low human-absorption percentage or as proof that the original food poses little exposure.
before.heading: Biomarkers, exposure and health outcomes

passages.text: The infant studies require careful study identity. The 2017 Belfast report includes 79 pre-weaning infants and an 11-infant paired subset. The separate 2018 New Hampshire study follows 15 paired infants and reports higher urinary arsenic species during weaning, with associations involving rice cereal, fruit and vegetables. These data support exposure investigation, but diet and age change together; the biomarker is not a rice-specific disease endpoint.

Du’s clinic cohort provides a useful null comparison: among 56 infants with reflux or dysphagia, total urinary arsenic did not differ statistically between thickener groups (p=0.086). The small, observational groups do not establish equivalence or justify changing prescribed feeding. A null thickener comparison also does not negate the dietary associations in a different cohort with different exposures and sampling.

Pregnancy adds physiological and metabolic complexity to urinary arsenic interpretation. Ashley-Martin’s review explains why species, timing, metabolism and exposure sources matter. A urine concentration should not be attributed to rice without considering drinking water and other foods, nor should urinary DMA automatically be equated with the amount of inorganic arsenic eaten.

after.text: Food concentrations, laboratory bioaccessibility and human biomarkers answer different questions. A chemical extraction yield is not a human absorption percentage. Infant and pregnancy studies support exposure investigation, but changes in diet, age, drinking water and metabolism complicate attribution to rice alone.
after.heading: Biomarkers, exposure and health outcomes

before.text: Rothenberg’s rural-China cohort links a prenatal exposure biomarker with child development, rather than measuring an intervention on rice. In adjusted models, doubling maternal hair total mercury corresponded to a 1.3-point lower mental-development score (95% CI −2.6 to −0.14); the psychomotor estimate’s interval included no association. Follow-up declined from 391 enrolled mothers to 190 children assessed at 36 months. Hair total mercury was the measured proxy, and attrition, caregiving and confounding limit a rice-specific causal interpretation.

passages.text: Modeled risk and observed disease must also remain separate. Song’s intake assessment multiplies food concentrations by consumption, while Huang’s meta-analysis includes hazard calculations whose combined-metal result must be distinguished from individual-metal quotients. These are exposure or risk models, not measured illness rates or a diagnosis for a reader. No individual risk prediction is generated from the occurrence explorer.

after.text: An ingredient concentration needs formulation, processing yield, preparation water and consumption data before it can inform an exposure estimate. Observational health associations do not establish that changing rice alone will change the outcome.

before.text: This is a structured comparative synthesis of selected ingested research, not a completed systematic review. It connects occurrence, mechanisms, interventions, product composition and human exposure while preserving their different study designs. The local evidence map also contains records whose exact findings remain unresolved. No pooled worldwide concentration, overall safety score or outcome-level certainty grade is assigned from publication counts.
before.heading: What this assessment establishes

passages.text: Several limitations can materially change the interpretation: reused global-survey samples and related experimental reports, uncertain processing bases, incomplete species preservation, and missing absolute residual effects or precision. Historical market samples do not establish current supplier performance. An association in a cohort does not establish that changing rice alone would alter the health outcome. These limits accompany the conclusions rather than being hidden in the source index.

The selected FDA and intervention explorers remain deliberately scoped to their reconciled datasets. The expanded narrative includes additional research whose observations have not all been reconciled into the same comparable row structure. Original tables, independent sample units, uncertainty and overlapping study families must be resolved before adding such findings to a quantitative comparison.

after.text: This review combines selected occurrence, intervention and exposure evidence. Question-specific screening and appraisal remain incomplete. The occurrence sidebars identify the admitted HMI references, original measurements and calculations; the Sources index also contains discovery records that have not been accepted as supporting evidence.
after.heading: What this assessment establishes

before.text: The most consequential remaining work concerns source accuracy and identity, compatible occurrence extraction, paired intervention residuals and uncertainty, species transformation during processing and storage, validated lot sampling, and exposure attribution. Several stored summaries contain conflicting arithmetic, species or compliance interpretations. The affected claims are withheld here; an unresolved extraction is not presented as proof that no evidence exists.
before.heading: Evidence still needed

passages.text: For agricultural controls, the next useful evidence is jointly measured residual Cd, iAs and relevant Hg species, alongside yield, nutrients, independent field units, durability, resource use and cost. For processing, it is a paired mass balance and species-preserving analysis of food and waste streams. For products and health, it is exact formulation and consumption context plus appropriately adjusted, uncertainty-bearing outcome estimates. These are specific limits on present decisions, rather than a demand for more papers regardless of relevance.

The starting inventory is the existing rice-linked source corpus, supplemented by targeted checks of original publications and authorities. Screening and question-specific external searching are incomplete; some original files are unavailable locally. The bibliography identifies the works actually used in the synthesis and explorers. The separate Sources index is a discovery aid and includes records that have not been accepted as supporting evidence.
passages.question: How were sources selected, and what does the source index mean?

passages.text: The evidence assessment was expanded on 18 October 2026 to distinguish global grain surveys from prepared-food composites, add species and derivative evidence, compare agronomic and processing controls including null findings, and connect food measurements with exposure and health research. New original data, corrected study identity, resolved overlap or material changes in requirements should reopen the affected conclusion.

after.text: The remaining gaps that most affect decisions are validated sampling for current lots, residual contamination and uncertainty after treatment, and commercial performance across sites and seasons. Unresolved source identity, measurement basis or shared samples can also prevent a finding from entering a quantitative reference.

before.text: Rice metal levels depend on growing conditions, grain form and preparation. Water management can trade lower inorganic arsenic for higher cadmium.

facets.label: Metals of concern
facets.text: [[metals/arsenic-inorganic|Inorganic arsenic]] and [[metals/cadmium|cadmium]] are central concerns. Lead, total mercury and chromium are also measured; chemical species remain separate.

facets.label: Main drivers
facets.text: Soil, cultivar and water management influence uptake. Bran retention, milling and cooking change the rice material being compared.

facets.label: Practical framing
facets.text: Keep grain and cooked-rice results separate. Excess-water cooking with the water discarded can lower inorganic arsenic; assess cadmium too and verify current supplier lots.
